newsitem.title: UK: Brent cash market eases, wet cargo trades quietly.
newsitem.headline: Brent cash market eases, wet cargo trades quietly.

text.p: The North Sea Brent cash market eased gently lower on Tuesday, while a wet trade done on a private and confidential basis was widely heard to be around five cents down on Monday's levels.
A European major confirmed that he had sold a Brent but the deal was kept private at the buyer's request. The loading dates were heard to be June 16-18.
Other traders speculated that the deal was done around July Brent -42 cents, after two cargoes were traded at July Brent -37 cents on Monday.
I think it's definitely looking weaker," said one.
At least two other wet Brent cargoes were being actively offered, dealers said.
Traders said that the transatlantic arbitrage was unworkable, with a July Brent/WTI spread of less than $1.50, and U.S. Gulf refiners' storage tanks full to the brim.
After the spread narrowed some 20-30 cents from late last week, Shell on Monday failed to fix the VLCC Berge Nisa for a transatlantic trip loading mid-June.
Two Brents loading June 18-20, one a deferral from June 14-16 were passing through the paper chains on Tuesday, traders said.
Other North Sea grades also had a softer tone, with talk focused on Ekofisk which traded twice on Monday.
A 500,000 barrel Ekofisk, loading June 19-21, traded on Tuesday at Dated Brent +17 cents, the lower end of Monday's range.
On the Brent paper market, intermonth spreads eased to talk at -22/-17 for June/July and -14/-11 for July/August.
CFDs were also slightly easier with next week (June 9-13) traded at July Brent -33 cents, and the following week (June 16-20) at August Brent -39 cents.
July Brent traded at $19.47 on the paper market and was trading at $19.45 on the IPE screen at 1224 GMT.

In the Mediterranean, traders said no deals were reported early on Tuesday but there was unconfirmed talk of a Urals cargo traded on Monday at Dated Brent -$1.35, four cents up on a deal last week for an end-May cargo.

Traders put sellers' levels for Urals at Dated Brent -$1.30 and buyers' at a five to 10 cents less than that. Some said buyers were holding back to see when the first Iraqi Kirkuk, which competes with Urals, will come out after U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Monday recommended a rollover of Iraq's $2 billion "oil-for-food" deal. "Refiners margins are sort of stable at the moment, they are not too bad but they are not brilliant. There is a wait-an see attitude from the buyers' side, waiting for Kirkuk to appear again," one Italian refiner said.

On a quiet West African market, traders said some July barrels were shown but added that sellers were still trying to clear unsold June cargoes. "There seems to be barrels that are left but they are basically U.S.-bound barrels. Maybe there's about 10 cargoes of Nigerian (crude) left unsold. Some of them are being shown in the (U.S.) Gulf coast," one trader said. The usual Far East buyers have not come in yet, with the trader saying "they may wait until the end of the week and then they start sniffing around". Most Nigerian grades were steady, with Bonny Light talked around Dated Brent +55 cents and Forcados at about a 25 cents premium to Dated Brent. The only grade a little pressured was Qua Iboe, with one seller reported to be still holding an unsold VLCC. Qua Iboe was assessed at Dated Brent +45 cents for June barrels while July were talked five cents higher.
--Ros Russell, Haitham Haddadin, London Newsroom +44 171 542 5387 (c) Reuters Limited 1997
